### `src/contexts/LanguageContext.jsx`

```jsx
import React, { createContext, useState, useContext, useEffect, useCallback } from 'react';
import { translations } from '../translations';
import { useAuth } from './AuthContext';
import { apiUrl } from '../config/api';

const LanguageContext = createContext();

const mapLanguageCode = (lang) => {
  // Map between frontend codes ('en', 'rw', 'fr') and database values ('English (UK)', etc.)
  const codeToDb = {
    'en': 'English (UK)',
    'rw': 'Kinyarwanda',
    'fr': 'French (France)'
  };
  const dbToCode = {
    'English (UK)': 'en',
    'Kinyarwanda': 'rw',
    'French (France)': 'fr'
  };
  if (codeToDb[lang]) return codeToDb[lang];
  if (dbToCode[lang]) return dbToCode[lang];
  return 'en';
};

export function LanguageProvider({ children }) {
  const { user, updateUser } = useAuth();
  const [language, setLanguageState] = useState('en');
  const [isSaving, setIsSaving] = useState(false);

  // Initialize language from user data when available
  useEffect(() => {
    if (user?.language) {
      const code = mapLanguageCode(user.language);
      setLanguageState(code);
    }
  }, [user?.language]);

  const setLanguage = useCallback(async (newLang) => {
    setLanguageState(newLang);
    if (user?.id) {
      setIsSaving(true);
      try {
        const token = localStorage.getItem('token');
        await fetch(apiUrl('/api/users/profile'), {
          method: 'PUT',
          headers: {
            'Content-Type': 'application/json',
            'Authorization': `Bearer ${token}`
          },
          body: JSON.stringify({
            language: mapLanguageCode(newLang)
          })
        });
        updateUser({ language: mapLanguageCode(newLang) });
      } catch (err) {
        console.error('Failed to save language preference:', err);
      } finally {
        setIsSaving(false);
      }
    }
  }, [user, updateUser]);

  const t = (key, params) => {
    const val = translations[language]?.[key] ?? translations.en?.[key] ?? key;
    // Guard: never return an object to React — fall back to key string
    if (val !== null && typeof val === 'object') return key;
    if (!params || typeof val !== 'string') return val;
    return val.replace(/\{(\w+)\}/g, (match, name) => (
      Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(params, name) && params[name] != null
        ? String(params[name])
        : match
    ));
  };

  return (
    <LanguageContext.Provider value={{ language, setLanguage, t, isSaving }}>
      {children}
    </LanguageContext.Provider>
  );
}

export function useLanguage() {
  const context = useContext(LanguageContext);
  if (!context) {
    throw new Error('useLanguage must be used within a LanguageProvider');
  }
  return context;
}
```

    "explorerCategory": "royal-historian",
    "content": "Before there were kings counted one after another, before there was a name for the land itself, the elders say there was only Gihanga — the one whose name comes from guhanga, \"to create.\" Every story about how Rwanda came to be a kingdom begins, in one way or another, with him. He is remembered less as a man who was born and grew old like other men, and more as the moment a scattered people first became a nation with a name.\n\nAs it is told, his line reached back further than any ordinary ancestry — through his father's side to a distant forefather named Kigwa, \"the one who descended,\" said to have come down from the heavens themselves to plant the royal line on earth. Whether the storyteller means this as memory or as metaphor for something too important to describe plainly has never mattered as much as what came after: a family marked, from its very beginning, as meant to lead.\n\nGihanga's own childhood was not an easy one. He was born, the elders say, in a time of disaster, and lost his father while still young. His mother carried him to her own grandfather's home, and it was there — away from where he might otherwise have been raised — that he grew into a boy so clever and so promising that he became his grandfather's favorite. A prophecy began to follow him quietly: that the throne of his forefathers would one day be his.\n\nA promise like that rarely goes unchallenged. His maternal uncle, watching the boy rise in favor and hearing the same prophecy repeated, was consumed by envy rather than pride. Rather than wait to see whether the prophecy was true, he began to scheme against the nephew who stood to inherit what he himself could not. Gihanga, still young, fled his uncle's reach together with a handful of loyal cousins — the first of several journeys that would carry him across unfamiliar territory before he ever ruled anything at all.\n\nIt was in his wandering, not in a palace, that Gihanga became the figure Rwandans still speak of today. Wherever he went, the stories say, he brought knowledge that a scattered people badly needed — the forging of iron, the shaping of wood, the working of clay into pottery, the keeping of fire, the raising of cattle. He was not only a claimant to a throne; he was, by every account, a craftsman first — a blacksmith's son who had learned his father's trade and carried it with him like a second inheritance.\n\nHe eventually made his way to Buhanga, a forest that would come to be remembered as sacred ground, and it was there that the scattered pieces of his journey became a kingdom. It was in Buhanga that he is said to have performed the rituals that marked his rule as legitimate, and where his first royal symbols were set — a hammer, for the craft that had carried him this far, and a musical instrument whose call was said to be able to seal the fate of the condemned. Later, tradition holds, one of his companions revealed to him the secret of a sacred royal drum — the beginning of what would become the Kalinga, the drum that would define Rwandan kingship for centuries afterward.\n\nPerhaps the most enduring symbol of all was the fire Gihanga lit at his court — a flame that, once kindled, was never meant to go out. For generations after him, it did not: kept burning through the reigns of kings who came long after his name had passed from memory into legend, a living sign that the kingdom he founded still stood. It would take colonial officials, centuries later, to finally order it extinguished — an act many Rwandans still describe not merely as political, but as an attempt to sever something the fire had always represented: an unbroken line between a people and their beginning.\n\nGihanga's story does not end tidily with a single victory or a single throne. It survives instead in fragments carried by different families, different clans, different court poets — some claiming descent from a son who inherited his kingdom, others from a daughter said to have brought the first cattle to Rwanda after a family dispute of her own. That every version disagrees on some detail and agrees on the shape of the whole is, in its own way, exactly how a founding story should survive: not as one fixed account, but as something every generation retells a little differently, because it still belongs to all of them."

      "en": "How a single string, threaded back and forth across a wooden trough, became the sound of Rwanda's royal court — anchored around Yuhi III Mazimpaka, remembered as a poet and inanga player.",
      "rw": "Uko umugozi umwe, uzengurutse mu kabaho k'igiti, wabaye ijwi ry'urukiko rw'ubwami bw'u Rwanda — hafatanyijwe n'Umwami Yuhi III Mazimpaka, wibukwa nk'umusizi n'umucuranzi w'inanga.",
      "fr": "Comment une seule corde, tissée d'un bout à l'autre d'une auge en bois, est devenue le son de la cour royale du Rwanda — centrée sur Yuhi III Mazimpaka, dont on se souvient comme d'un poète et joueur d'inanga."
    },
    "duration": "7 min read",
    "durationSec": 420,
    "imageKey": "inanga",
    "audioUrl": "",
    "youtubeRef": "",
    "storyId": "inanga-mazimpaka",
    "category": "Traditional music",
    "explorerCategory": "music-explorer",
    "content": "Long before speakers and stages, the sound that carried Rwanda's history was startlingly simple: one long string, threaded back and forth across notches cut into a hollowed wooden trough, plucked by a single pair of hands. That instrument is the inanga, and for centuries it has been considered one of the most revered instruments in Rwandan life — not because of volume or complexity, but because of what it was trusted to carry: memory itself.\n\nThe inanga's design hides its cleverness in plain sight. What looks like six to eight separate strings is often just one continuous length, woven across a series of carved notches at either end of the trough, then tuned string by string with small wooden pegs. Seated with the instrument resting against the lap, a player plucks out a repeating, pentatonic melody — and it's over that gentle, looping foundation that the real performance begins: a voice, half-sung and half-whispered, carrying stories of history, personal experience, or the ordinary events of daily life.\n\nIn Rwanda's royal courts, the inanga held a place few instruments anywhere are given — it was played for kings, trusted to praise them, and trusted just as often to record them. Among the names still remembered from that tradition is Yuhi III Mazimpaka, a king of the early eighteenth century remembered less for conquest than for a rarer kind of reputation: a brilliant poet and skilled musician in his own right, said to have used his gift to tell the story of his own kingdom's rise.\n\nThat a king would be remembered as a performer, rather than only as a ruler, says something about how central this tradition was to Rwandan court life. The inanga wasn't background music — it was one of the primary ways history moved from one generation to the next, through ibitekerezo, epic poems recounting the deeds of kings and dynasties, composed and performed with the same instrument used for quieter, personal songs about love, loss, or the passing of ordinary days.\n\nThe whispery, murmuring singing style that traditionally accompanies the inanga — sometimes called kwivuga — was deliberately understated, almost private, even when performed for a king. Listeners didn't always catch every word; the lyrics often carried layered or hidden meanings meant to be interpreted rather than simply heard. In many ways, the instrument's quiet character was the point: history told gently is still history remembered.\n\nThe inanga's story didn't end with the royal courts. It survived colonization, cultural upheaval, and — after 1994 — the task of helping a country rebuild a shared cultural identity in the wake of unimaginable loss. Musicians like Thomas Kirusu and his daughter Sophie Nzayisenga, among Rwanda's most celebrated inanga players in recent generations, carried the instrument forward into a new era, proving it could hold both grief and unity in the same strings that once praised kings.\n\nToday the inanga still rests in players' laps the same way it did centuries ago, still tuned by hand, still accompanied by that same soft, half-sung voice. It remains, as it always has, less an instrument for performance and more a vessel — one string, threaded back and forth, carrying forward whatever a person trusts it to remember."
  },

Where her father's story is one of thrones and prophecies, hers is a smaller story, about a single household and a single unfamiliar animal — and yet it is the story Rwandans still credit for one of the most treasured things in their culture: the cow.\n\nAs it is told, Nyirarucyaba did not grow up in easy peace.     "content": "Of all the figures carried through Rwanda's oral tradition, none belongs to the wild places quite like Ryangombe. Where kings are remembered for courts and conquests, Ryangombe is remembered for forests, hunts, and mountains — a hero whose whole story unfolds not behind palace walls, but out among the hills, the game trails, and the volcanoes that still rise along Rwanda's northern border.\n\nThe elders say he came originally from Kitara, in what is now western Uganda, arriving in Rwanda generations ago as a young man already known for his skill in the hunt. He was not born into the throne the way Rwanda's kings were — his reputation was built entirely out in the wilderness, tracking game through forest and grassland until his name for courage and skill traveled faster than he did.\n\nIt was on one such hunt, the story goes, that everything changed. Deep in a forest, Ryangombe is said to have come upon a sacred grove unlike any other — a place where the boundary between the ordinary world and something older and larger grew thin. There, spirits are said to have recognized in him a kind of greatness the forest itself had been waiting for, and offered him a place among them.\n\nWhat makes Ryangombe's story endure isn't a single act of bravery, but the way he is remembered afterward — as jovial rather than distant, fond of music, dance, and feasting as much as the hunt, a spirit closer to the people who honored him than the fiercer, more fearsome figures found in other traditions. Communities who kept his memory alive did so not out of fear, but out of a sense that he understood the wild world better than almost anyone, and could be trusted to look after those who respected it.\n\nHis story ends, as many old hunting tales do, out in the field — struck down during a hunt, his companions said to have grieved him so deeply that his memory was carried forward not as an ending, but as a beginning. From that day, the elders say, Ryangombe made his home in Karisimbi, one of the great Virunga volcanoes that still stand along Rwanda's northern edge — visible, on a clear day, from almost anywhere in the country.\n\nThat detail is worth sitting with for a moment: of all the places a legendary figure could be said to dwell, Ryangombe's story chose a volcano — visible, permanent, part of the landscape itself. For generations, communities who honored his memory treated Karisimbi the way some cultures treat a temple spire: a constant, shared point on the horizon, a reminder that some stories don't need walls to be remembered. Even now, some communities continue to honor traditions connected to his memory, a living thread between old forests and the present day.\n\nWhatever else his story carries, the throughline is this: Ryangombe belonged to the wild places first, and only became a legend because he refused to be separated from them. For anyone drawn to Rwanda's forests, hills, and volcanoes today, his story is a reminder that this landscape has always been more than scenery — it has been, for as long as these stories have been told, a place people believed was watching back."

### `src/data/proverbs.json`

```json
{
  "_comment": "Rwandan proverbs (imigani) and riddles (ibisakuzo) for the popup card widget. rw = original Kinyarwanda, en = English translation, fr = French translation, meaning = interpretive gloss, source = reference numbers from original collection.",
  "proverbs": [
    {"id":"p001","rw":"Amategeko arusha amabuye kuremera","en":"Laws are heavier than stones.","fr":"Les lois sont plus lourdes que les pierres.","meaning":"Laws require impossible architects.","source":"558, 101"},
    {"id":"p002","rw":"Nta ho bucyikera n'ikuzimu baraganya","en":"There isn't a place where peace reigns at night.","fr":"Il n'y a pas d'endroit où la paix règne la nuit.","meaning":"Peace exists nowhere.","source":"2275, 333"},
    {"id":"p003","rw":"Umugani ntuva ku busa","en":"A proverb never comes as if from nowhere.","fr":"Un proverbe ne vient jamais de nulle part.","meaning":"All proverbs have a good reason for existing.","source":"3340, 470"},
    {"id":"p004","rw":"Zirara zishya bwacya zikazima","en":"(Homes) might burn all night, they always go off in the morning.","fr":"(Les maisons) peuvent brûler toute la nuit, elles s'éteignent toujours au matin.","meaning":"All conflicts eventually die down.","source":"4451, 619"},
    {"id":"p005","rw":"Ijya gucura indi yiyita nkuru","en":"The one that grabs a larger portion pretends to be the eldest.","fr":"Celui qui prend la plus grande part prétend être l'aîné.","meaning":"There is no stopping the exploitation of the other.","source":"1106, 174"},
    {"id":"p006","rw":"Inda y'undi itera induru ntibabimenye","en":"The other's belly cries and no one hears it.","fr":"Le ventre de l'autre pleure et personne ne l'entend.","meaning":"The other's suffering is incomprehensible.","source":"1509, 227"},
    {"id":"p007","rw":"Izina si lyo muntu","en":"A name isn't a man.","fr":"Un nom n'est pas un homme.","meaning":"A name says nothing of a person.","source":"2051, 302"},
    {"id":"p008","rw":"Nta bubyimba bw'inda bupfa ubusa","en":"There is no pregnancy that isn't useful.","fr":"Il n'y a pas de grossesse qui ne soit utile.","meaning":"Said after a fruitless pregnancy.","source":"2250, 330"},
    {"id":"p009","rw":"Nta gise kiba igisasa","en":"The pain of giving birth is never mediocre.","fr":"La douleur de l'accouchement n'est jamais banale.","meaning":"Children are always useful, even born-dead.","source":"2273, 333"},
    {"id":"p010","rw":"Nyina w'umuntu agira ake kezi","en":"Someone's mother always comes first.","fr":"La mère de quelqu'un passe toujours en premier.","meaning":"A beloved should always be respected.","source":"2667, 381"},
    {"id":"p011","rw":"Umusonga w'undi ntukubuza gusinzira","en":"The other's stitch in the side doesn't prevent you from sleeping.","fr":"Le point de côté de l'autre ne t'empêche pas de dormir.","meaning":"One never notices the other's misfortunes.","source":"3634, 510"},
    {"id":"p012","rw":"Urusha nyina w'umwana imbabazi aba ashaka kumulya","en":"The one who professes more compassion than a mother tries to eat the child.","fr":"Celui qui professe plus de compassion qu'une mère cherche à dévorer l'enfant.","meaning":"No one can be more generous than a mother.","source":"3926, 549"},
    {"id":"p013","rw":"Akarenze impinga karushya ihamagara","en":"What reaches the top of the hill cannot be called back.","fr":"Ce qui atteint le sommet de la colline ne peut plus être rappelé.","meaning":"What is said can sometimes have terrible consequences.","source":"406, 81"},
    {"id":"p014","rw":"Ifumbire y'ubucuti ni amagambo","en":"The fertilizer of friendship is made of words.","fr":"L'engrais de l'amitié est fait de paroles.","meaning":"Peace can only take place through the power of words.","source":"977, 157"},
    {"id":"p015","rw":"Mvuge ligende","en":"Speech travels enough.","fr":"La parole voyage suffisamment.","meaning":"Anti-phrase used to caution against speaking too much.","source":"2192, 322"},
    {"id":"p016","rw":"Nta bisanganwa nk'amagambo","en":"Nothing else but speech.","fr":"Rien d'autre que la parole.","meaning":"To have nothing else to offer but speech.","source":"2247, 330"},
    {"id":"p017","rw":"Injunga y'urulimi inesha injunga z'igitero","en":"The sharpness of the tongue defeats the sharpness of the warriors.","fr":"La tranchant de la langue surpasse le tranchant des guerriers.","meaning":"Language is better than weapons.","source":"1602, 239"},
    {"id":"p018","rw":"Kurarama si ko kuramukanya","en":"To raise the eyes isn't to greet the other.","fr":"Lever les yeux n'est pas saluer l'autre.","meaning":"The eyes show no real effort to welcome the other; refers to hypocrisy.","source":"2121, 311"},
    {"id":"p019","rw":"Libera kurora","en":"The eye is for looking.","fr":"L'œil est fait pour voir.","meaning":"Emphasizes the function of the eye.","source":"2140, 314"},
    {"id":"p020","rw":"Mayenya imenya isuku ishyize imbere aliko ntimenya umwanda isize inyuma","en":"The slug is aware of the cleanliness ahead, never the dirt left behind.","fr":"La limace voit la propreté devant elle, jamais la saleté laissée derrière.","meaning":"One cannot preach what one doesn't practice.","source":"2151, 316"},
    {"id":"p021","rw":"Agacumu kazaguhorera ntumenya uwagacuze","en":"You never know who will make the spade that will avenge you.","fr":"On ne sait jamais qui forgera la bêche qui te vengera.","meaning":"The future is always uncertain.","source":"82, 38"},
    {"id":"p022","rw":"Amaziro n'amaciro birangana","en":"Ends and beginnings are identical.","fr":"Les fins et les débuts sont identiques.","meaning":"There is no true origin.","source":"574, 103"},
    {"id":"p023","rw":"Iby'ejo bibara ab'ejo","en":"Tomorrow's things are told by those coming tomorrow.","fr":"Les choses de demain sont racontées par ceux qui viennent demain.","meaning":"The future belongs to no one.","source":"899, 148"},
    {"id":"p024","rw":"Imana iraguha ntimugura iyo muguze iraguhenda","en":"Imana gives without a deal; if you deal, it will cost you.","fr":"Imana donne sans marchandage; si tu marchandes, cela te coûtera.","meaning":"The future is ungrateful.","source":"1214, 187"},
    {"id":"p025","rw":"Nta muhanuzi mu babo","en":"No prophet amongst ourselves.","fr":"Pas de prophète parmi les nôtres.","meaning":"No one can guess the future.","source":"2324, 339"},
    {"id":"p026","rw":"Nta wutinya ijoro atinya icyo balihuliye mo","en":"No one fears the night; one fears what steps out of it.","fr":"Personne ne craint la nuit; on craint ce qui en sort.","meaning":"The unknown isn't frightening — what lurks inside it is.","source":"2336, 363"},
    {"id":"p027","rw":"Ntibarufata","en":"One never holds death.","fr":"On ne retient jamais la mort.","meaning":"Death always comes unexpectedly.","source":"2563, 367"},
    {"id":"p028","rw":"Rusigariye abaseka","en":"Death holds itself in readiness for the ones who laugh.","fr":"La mort se tient prête pour ceux qui rient.","meaning":"Death should not be laughed at.","source":"2730, 390"},
    {"id":"p029","rw":"Ukize inkuba arayiganira","en":"To escape thunder is to speak about it.","fr":"Échapper au tonnerre, c'est en parler.","meaning":"Danger can only be talked about once it is over.","source":"3155, 446"},
    {"id":"p030","rw":"Nta wanga ilya mukuru","en":"No one can discard an elder's saying.","fr":"Personne ne peut rejeter la parole d'un aîné.","meaning":"Elders tell the future.","source":"2406, 346"},
    {"id":"p031","rw":"Abakiranye bakundana berekana imyobo","en":"Wrestlers that love one another show each other where the holes are.","fr":"Les lutteurs qui s'aiment se montrent mutuellement où sont les failles.","meaning":"Love and hatred never co-exist.","source":"32, 31"},
    {"id":"p032","rw":"Aho ubuhoro buli umuhoro urogosha","en":"Where there is peace, daggers are used for shaving.","fr":"Là où règne la paix, les poignards servent à se raser.","meaning":"There is no such thing as absolute peace.","source":"254, 61"},
    {"id":"p033","rw":"Intobyi y'amaraso irayitera","en":"The destiny of two fingers is to live together.","fr":"Le destin de deux doigts est de vivre ensemble.","meaning":"Co-habitation cannot be evaded.","source":"1795, 267"},
    {"id":"p034","rw":"Ubushiki ni ubulibwa","en":"A sibling's relation is one that consumes itself.","fr":"La relation fraternelle est celle qui se consume.","meaning":"Fraternity has nothing to do with blood; it has to do with dialogue.","source":"2849, 407"},
    {"id":"p035","rw":"Umuvandimwe wa kure arutwa n'umuturanyi","en":"A distant brother is less valuable than a neighbor.","fr":"Un frère lointain vaut moins qu'un voisin proche.","meaning":"The other who is close is more important than a distant sibling.","source":"3692, 519"},
    {"id":"p036","rw":"Urugo rutuboye irembo ikije nyira rwo arakira","en":"From within a courtyard, the owner welcomes all that comes.","fr":"Depuis la cour, le propriétaire accueille tout ce qui vient.","meaning":"Hospitality has to be absolute — it cannot be relative.","source":"3880, 543"},
    {"id":"p037","rw":"Uwabonye ikirago alilira umuraza","en":"The one who finds bedding aspires for a bed-mate.","fr":"Celui qui trouve une literie aspire à un compagnon de lit.","meaning":"Once a need is satisfied, another arises.","source":"4220, 588"},
    {"id":"p038","rw":"Indinde iba kabili","en":"\"Wait for me\" always takes place twice.","fr":"\"Attends-moi\" se produit toujours deux fois.","meaning":"One is never alone.","source":"1513, 227"},
    {"id":"p039","rw":"Ingingo y'ijambo iva mu ijigo","en":"The depth of a speech comes with jaws.","fr":"La profondeur d'un discours vient avec les mâchoires.","meaning":"There is no escaping the body.","source":"1564, 234"},
    {"id":"p040","rw":"Umuntu asimbuka iminsi ntasimbuka umunsi","en":"One lives through the day, one never steps beyond the day.","fr":"On traverse les jours, on ne dépasse jamais le jour présent.","meaning":"There is only the present.","source":"3528, 497"},
    {"id":"p041","rw":"Umunyurwa araguma","en":"The grateful is rare.","fr":"Le reconnaissant est rare.","meaning":"One is often let down by the other.","source":"3558, 501"},
    {"id":"p042","rw":"Umushumba w'inda ntasinzira","en":"The stomach never lets go.","fr":"L'estomac ne lâche jamais prise.","meaning":"Survival implies struggle.","source":"3624, 509"},
    {"id":"p043","rw":"Umusogongero w'itsi ni umubano","en":"Savoring the world only takes place when you get along.","fr":"Savourer le monde ne se fait que lorsqu'on s'entend bien.","meaning":"The world makes no sense without friendship.","source":"3632, 510"},
    {"id":"p044","rw":"Wanga kwiruka ukagwira ubusa","en":"You refuse to run and there goes your fall.","fr":"Tu refuses de courir et voilà ta chute.","meaning":"Nothing is gained without risk.","source":"4415, 614"},
    {"id":"p045","rw":"Hapfa uwavutse","en":"Dies who is born.","fr":"Meurt celui qui est né.","meaning":"Death is already the fate of the one who is born.","source":"791, 133"},
    {"id":"p046","rw":"Iliboneye ntilyica","en":"The straight arrow doesn't always kill.","fr":"La flèche droite ne tue pas toujours.","meaning":"Destiny can never be controlled — a crooked arrow can kill too.","source":"1180, 183"},
    {"id":"p047","rw":"Nta wucika yenda","en":"No one can stop one's lineage.","fr":"Personne ne peut arrêter sa lignée.","meaning":"Every person seeks to survive through their children.","source":"2441, 353"},
    {"id":"p048","rw":"Udasize umwana asiga umugani","en":"Whoever doesn't leave a child, leaves behind a proverb.","fr":"Celui qui ne laisse pas d'enfant laisse un proverbe.","meaning":"Lineage isn't the only legacy.","source":"2980, 423"},
    {"id":"p049","rw":"Ujya gupfa abanziliza ku bugaboo","en":"Whoever dies is first affected in their ability to reproduce.","fr":"Celui qui va mourir est d'abord atteint dans sa capacité à se reproduire.","meaning":"Death is nothing so long as one survives through one's children.","source":"3113, 440"},
    {"id":"p050","rw":"Zimungira ukubili aliko zigahuliza imbere","en":"Beetles chew from either side, but always end up together inside.","fr":"Les scarabées mâchent des deux côtés, mais finissent toujours ensemble à l'intérieur.","meaning":"There is no point acting alone when the aim is shared by all.","source":"4446, 618"}
    ,{"id":"p051","rw":"Akimuhana kaza imvura ihise","en":"Help from far away arrives after the rain has passed.","fr":"L'aide venue de loin arrive apres la pluie.","meaning":"Local help is often more useful than distant promises.","meaningRw":"Ubufasha bwa hafi bugira umumaro kurusha amasezerano ya kure.","meaningFr":"L'aide proche vaut mieux que les promesses lointaines.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p052","rw":"Amaboko atareshya araramukanya","en":"Unequal hands still greet each other.","fr":"Des mains inegales se saluent quand meme.","meaning":"People of different status still need one another.","meaningRw":"Abantu badahuje ubushobozi cyangwa icyubahiro baracyakenerana.","meaningFr":"Des personnes de rang different ont toujours besoin les unes des autres.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p053","rw":"Igiti kigororwa kikiri gito","en":"A tree is straightened while it is still young.","fr":"L'arbre se redresse quand il est encore jeune.","meaning":"Good character is taught early.","meaningRw":"Uburere bwiza butangirwa umuntu akiri muto.","meaningFr":"Le bon caractere se forme tot.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p054","rw":"Inkingi imwe ntigera inzu","en":"One pillar cannot hold up a house.","fr":"Un seul pilier ne soutient pas une maison.","meaning":"Shared work is stronger than solitary effort.","meaningRw":"Igikorwa kirakomera iyo abantu bagishyize hamwe.","meaningFr":"Le travail partage est plus solide que l'effort solitaire.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p055","rw":"Abishyize hamwe nta kibananira","en":"Those who unite are not defeated by anything.","fr":"Ceux qui s'unissent ne sont vaincus par rien.","meaning":"Unity makes difficult work possible.","meaningRw":"Ubumwe butuma ibikomeye bishoboka.","meaningFr":"L'unite rend possible ce qui est difficile.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p056","rw":"Uburere buruta ubuvuke","en":"Upbringing is greater than birth.","fr":"L'education vaut mieux que la naissance.","meaning":"Character matters more than family origin.","meaningRw":"Imyitwarire iruta inkomoko umuntu yavukiyemo.","meaningFr":"Le caractere compte plus que l'origine familiale.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p057","rw":"Ijambo ryiza ni mugenzi w'Imana","en":"A good word is a companion of God.","fr":"Une bonne parole accompagne Dieu.","meaning":"Kind speech brings peace and dignity.","meaningRw":"Ijambo ryiza rizana amahoro n'icyubahiro.","meaningFr":"Une parole bienveillante apporte paix et dignite.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p058","rw":"Ijoro ribara uwariraye","en":"The night is understood by the one who spent it awake.","fr":"La nuit est comprise par celui qui l'a veillee.","meaning":"Only the person who lived a hardship fully knows it.","meaningRw":"Uwahuye n'ikibazo ni we umenya uburemere bwacyo.","meaningFr":"Seule la personne qui a vecu l'epreuve la connait vraiment.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p059","rw":"Utaganiriye na se ntamenya icyo sekuru yasize avuze","en":"Whoever does not speak with his father cannot know what his grandfather said.","fr":"Qui ne parle pas a son pere ignore ce que son grand-pere a dit.","meaning":"Heritage is preserved through conversation between generations.","meaningRw":"Umurage ubikwa mu biganiro hagati y'abakuru n'abato.","meaningFr":"Le patrimoine se conserve par le dialogue entre generations.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p060","rw":"Utagira mukuru agira Imana","en":"One without an elder still has God.","fr":"Celui qui n'a pas d'aine a toujours Dieu.","meaning":"When human guidance is absent, hope can still remain.","meaningRw":"Iyo ubujyanama bw'abantu bubuze, icyizere kiracyabaho.","meaningFr":"Quand le conseil humain manque, l'espoir demeure.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p061","rw":"Uwitonze akama ishashi","en":"The patient person can milk a heifer.","fr":"La personne patiente peut traire une genisse.","meaning":"Patience can make difficult tasks succeed.","meaningRw":"Kwihangana no kwitonda bituma ibikomeye bishoboka.","meaningFr":"La patience permet de reussir les taches difficiles.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p062","rw":"Ujya kurisha ihera ku rugo","en":"One who goes to graze begins from home.","fr":"Celui qui va faire paitre commence a la maison.","meaning":"Good work begins with responsibilities close to you.","meaningRw":"Umurimo mwiza utangirira ku nshingano zikwegereye.","meaningFr":"Le bon travail commence par les responsabilites proches.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p063","rw":"Agahinda k'inkoko kamenywa n'inkike yatoyemo","en":"The sorrow of the hen is known by the fence where it scratched.","fr":"La peine de la poule se voit a la cloture ou elle a gratte.","meaning":"Pain often leaves signs before it is spoken.","meaningRw":"Agahinda k'umuntu kagaragarira mu bimenyetso mbere yo kukavuga.","meaningFr":"La peine laisse souvent des signes avant d'etre dite.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p064","rw":"Nta nkumi yigaya","en":"No maiden criticizes herself.","fr":"Aucune jeune fille ne se critique elle-meme.","meaning":"People rarely see their own faults clearly.","meaningRw":"Umuntu abona amakosa ye bigoranye.","meaningFr":"On voit rarement ses propres defauts clairement.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p065","rw":"Umwana apfa mu iterura","en":"A child is harmed in the way they are carried.","fr":"Un enfant souffre selon la facon dont on le porte.","meaning":"Careless care can injure the vulnerable.","meaningRw":"Kwita ku muntu nabi bishobora kumugirira nabi kurusha kumufasha.","meaningFr":"Un soin maladroit peut blesser les plus vulnerables.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p066","rw":"Umutwe umwe ntiwigira inama","en":"One head does not advise itself.","fr":"Une seule tete ne se conseille pas elle-meme.","meaning":"Wisdom grows through consultation.","meaningRw":"Ubwenge bwiyongera iyo abantu bajya inama.","meaningFr":"La sagesse grandit par la consultation.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p067","rw":"Irya mukuru riraryoha riryoha","en":"An elder's word is sweet again and again.","fr":"La parole d'un aine reste douce encore et encore.","meaning":"Elders' advice keeps its value over time.","meaningRw":"Inama z'abakuru zigumana agaciro uko igihe gihita.","meaningFr":"Le conseil des anciens garde sa valeur avec le temps.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p068","rw":"Akanwa karya ntikavuge","en":"The mouth that eats should not speak carelessly.","fr":"La bouche qui mange ne parle pas avec legerete.","meaning":"Gratitude requires discretion and respect.","meaningRw":"Gushimira bisaba kwitonda no kubaha.","meaningFr":"La gratitude demande discretion et respect.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p069","rw":"Ururimi rutagira amagufwa ruvuna amagufwa","en":"The boneless tongue breaks bones.","fr":"La langue sans os brise les os.","meaning":"Words can wound more deeply than force.","meaningRw":"Amagambo ashobora gukomeretsa kurusha imbaraga.","meaningFr":"Les mots peuvent blesser plus que la force.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p070","rw":"Nta wumenya aho bwira ageze","en":"No one knows where night will find them.","fr":"Nul ne sait ou la nuit le trouvera.","meaning":"The future is uncertain, so humility is wise.","meaningRw":"Ejo hazaza ntihamenyekana, ni byiza kwicisha bugufi.","meaningFr":"L'avenir est incertain, donc l'humilite est sage.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p071","rw":"Inzira ntibwira umugenzi","en":"The road does not warn the traveler.","fr":"La route ne previent pas le voyageur.","meaning":"Experience teaches what advice may not reveal.","meaningRw":"Ubunararibonye bwigisha ibyo inama itabasha kwerekana.","meaningFr":"L'experience enseigne ce que le conseil ne revele pas toujours.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p072","rw":"Umutima muhanano ntiwuzura igituza","en":"A borrowed heart does not fill the chest.","fr":"Un coeur emprunte ne remplit pas la poitrine.","meaning":"Borrowed courage cannot replace inner conviction.","meaningRw":"Ubutwari bw'ugutira ntibusimbura ukwemera kuva imbere.","meaningFr":"Le courage emprunte ne remplace pas la conviction interieure.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p073","rw":"Uko zivuze ni ko zitambirwa","en":"Drums are danced to as they sound.","fr":"On danse selon le son des tambours.","meaning":"People respond according to the situation before them.","meaningRw":"Abantu bitwara bakurikije uko ibihe bimeze.","meaningFr":"On agit selon la situation presente.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p074","rw":"Aho umutima ushaka amaguru ajyana","en":"Where the heart desires, the feet go.","fr":"La ou le coeur desire, les pieds vont.","meaning":"Desire often directs action.","meaningRw":"Icyifuzo cy'umutima gikurura ibikorwa by'umuntu.","meaningFr":"Le desir oriente souvent l'action.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p075","rw":"Uwariye umunyu ntiyibagirwa amazi","en":"Whoever ate salt does not forget water.","fr":"Qui a mange du sel n'oublie pas l'eau.","meaning":"A need teaches lasting gratitude.","meaningRw":"Ubukene cyangwa inyota bigisha gushimira ibikenewe.","meaningFr":"Le besoin enseigne une gratitude durable.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p076","rw":"Akaryoshye ntigahora mu itama","en":"A sweet thing does not remain forever in the cheek.","fr":"Une chose douce ne reste pas toujours dans la joue.","meaning":"Pleasure is temporary, so enjoy it with measure.","meaningRw":"Ibinezeza ntibiramba; bikwiye kwakirwa mu rugero.","meaningFr":"Le plaisir est passager; il faut le vivre avec mesure.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p077","rw":"Agatinze kazaza ni amenyo ya ruguru","en":"What delays but surely comes is the upper teeth.","fr":"Ce qui tarde mais vient surement, ce sont les dents du haut.","meaning":"Some outcomes require patience.","meaningRw":"Hari ibigerwaho bisaba gutegereza.","meaningFr":"Certains resultats exigent de la patience.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p078","rw":"Aho rukomeye ni ho rukomeza","en":"Where the rope is strong, it is tightened.","fr":"La ou la corde est solide, on la serre davantage.","meaning":"Trust grows where reliability has already been shown.","meaningRw":"Icyizere cyiyongera aho ubudahemuka bwagaragaye.","meaningFr":"La confiance grandit la ou la fiabilite est prouvee.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p079","rw":"Uwarose nabi burinda bucya","en":"Whoever had a bad dream waits anxiously for morning.","fr":"Qui a fait un mauvais reve attend le matin avec inquietude.","meaning":"Fear makes time feel longer.","meaningRw":"Ubwoba butuma igihe gisa n'ikitagenda.","meaningFr":"La peur rend le temps plus long.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p080","rw":"Umurimo unoze ugaragaza nyirawo","en":"Well-done work reveals its maker.","fr":"Un travail bien fait revele son auteur.","meaning":"Quality carries the signature of character.","meaningRw":"Umurimo unoze ugaragaza imyitwarire ya nyirawo.","meaningFr":"La qualite porte la signature du caractere.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p081","rw":"Nyiri ukuboko ni we umenya aho kurambukira","en":"The owner of the arm knows where to stretch it.","fr":"Le proprietaire du bras sait ou l'etendre.","meaning":"Each person knows their own capacity best.","meaningRw":"Buri muntu ni we umenya ubushobozi bwe kurusha abandi.","meaningFr":"Chacun connait mieux sa propre capacite.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p082","rw":"Umuco utagira abawuvuga urazima","en":"A culture without people to speak it fades.","fr":"Une culture sans voix pour la dire s'eteint.","meaning":"Heritage survives when people continue to share it.","meaningRw":"Umuco ukomeza kubaho iyo abantu bawuvuga kandi bawusangira.","meaningFr":"Le patrimoine survit quand les gens continuent a le partager.","source":"Umuco Core archive"},
    {"id":"p083","rw":"Amateka atabitswe aratwarwa n'umuyaga","en":"Unpreserved history is carried away by the wind.","fr":"L'histoire non conservee est emportee par le vent.","meaning":"Memory needs care, records, and witnesses.","meaningRw":"Urwibutso rukenera kurindwa, kwandikwa no guhamywa.","meaningFr":"La memoire a besoin de soin, d'archives et de temoins.","source":"Umuco Core archive"},
    {"id":"p084","rw":"Uwumva neza abika kabiri","en":"Whoever listens well preserves twice.","fr":"Qui ecoute bien conserve deux fois.","meaning":"Deep listening protects both words and meaning.","meaningRw":"Gutega amatwi neza birinda amagambo n'ubusobanuro bwayo.","meaningFr":"Une ecoute attentive preserve les mots et leur sens.","source":"Umuco Core archive"},
    {"id":"p085","rw":"Icyo abakuru babitse ni cyo abato baheraho","en":"What elders preserve becomes the beginning for the young.","fr":"Ce que les anciens gardent devient le depart des jeunes.","meaning":"Each generation builds from inherited memory.","meaningRw":"Buri gisekuru cyubakira ku murage cyasigiwe.","meaningFr":"Chaque generation construit a partir de la memoire recue.","source":"Umuco Core archive"},
    {"id":"p086","rw":"Umugani uvuzwe neza uba ishuri","en":"A well-told proverb becomes a school.","fr":"Un proverbe bien dit devient une ecole.","meaning":"Short sayings can carry deep teaching.","meaningRw":"Amagambo make ashobora gutwara inyigisho ndende.","meaningFr":"De courtes paroles peuvent porter un grand enseignement.","source":"Umuco Core archive"},
    {"id":"p087","rw":"Umenya igihugu aciye mu rurimi rwacyo","en":"One knows a country by passing through its language.","fr":"On connait un pays en passant par sa langue.","meaning":"Language opens the inner life of a culture.","meaningRw":"Ururimi rufungura ubuzima bw'imbere bw'umuco.","meaningFr":"La langue ouvre la vie interieure d'une culture.","source":"Umuco Core archive"},
    {"id":"p088","rw":"Ijwi ry'umukuru ntirisaza mu matwi y'abato","en":"An elder's voice does not grow old in the ears of the young.","fr":"La voix d'un ancien ne vieillit pas aux oreilles des jeunes.","meaning":"Good counsel remains fresh across generations.","meaningRw":"Inama nziza ikomeza kuba nshya mu bisekuru byose.","meaningFr":"Un bon conseil reste vivant entre les generations.","source":"Umuco Core archive"},
    {"id":"p089","rw":"Uwigisha umwana aba yubaka ejo","en":"Whoever teaches a child is building tomorrow.","fr":"Qui enseigne un enfant construit demain.","meaning":"Education shapes the future community.","meaningRw":"Uburere bw'umwana bwubaka umuryango w'ejo hazaza.","meaningFr":"L'education forme la communaute de demain.","source":"Umuco Core archive"},
    {"id":"p090","rw":"Akari ku mutima gasesekara ku munwa","en":"What is in the heart spills onto the mouth.","fr":"Ce qui est dans le coeur deborde sur la bouche.","meaning":"Speech often reveals hidden feeling.","meaningRw":"Imvugo y'umuntu akenshi igaragaza ibiri ku mutima.","meaningFr":"La parole revele souvent le sentiment cache.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p091","rw":"Umunsi mwiza uhera mu gitondo","en":"A good day begins in the morning.","fr":"Une bonne journee commence le matin.","meaning":"Early effort shapes later results.","meaningRw":"Imbaraga za kare zigira uruhare ku musaruro w'umunsi.","meaningFr":"L'effort du matin influence les resultats du jour.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p092","rw":"Nta mugabo umwe wigira igihugu","en":"No single person becomes a country.","fr":"Une seule personne ne devient pas un pays.","meaning":"A nation is made through many lives and duties.","meaningRw":"Igihugu cyubakwa n'abantu benshi n'inshingano basangiye.","meaningFr":"Une nation se fait par de nombreuses vies et responsabilites.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p093","rw":"Uwakiriye neza aba abitse inzira","en":"Whoever welcomes well preserves the road.","fr":"Qui accueille bien preserve le chemin.","meaning":"Hospitality keeps relationships open.","meaningRw":"Kwakira neza bituma umubano n'inzira bikomeza gufunguka.","meaningFr":"L'hospitalite garde les relations ouvertes.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p094","rw":"Umurage utavuzwe ucika nk'umugozi ushaje","en":"Unspoken heritage snaps like an old rope.","fr":"Un patrimoine non raconte casse comme une vieille corde.","meaning":"Traditions must be retold to remain alive.","meaningRw":"Imigenzo igomba kuvugwa kenshi kugira ngo ikomeze kubaho.","meaningFr":"Les traditions doivent etre racontees pour rester vivantes.","source":"Umuco Core archive"},
    {"id":"p095","rw":"Akabando k'iminsi gacibwa kare kakabikwa kure","en":"The walking stick for future days is cut early and kept safely.","fr":"Le baton des jours a venir se coupe tot et se garde loin.","meaning":"Prepare early for future need.","meaningRw":"Tegura kare ibyo uzakenera mu minsi iri imbere.","meaningFr":"Prepare tot ce dont l'avenir aura besoin.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p096","rw":"Umuti w'ubukene ni ugukora","en":"The cure for poverty is work.","fr":"Le remede a la pauvrete, c'est le travail.","meaning":"Dignified effort is the first answer to lack.","meaningRw":"Gukora mu cyubahiro ni intambwe ya mbere yo guhangana n'ubukene.","meaningFr":"L'effort digne est la premiere reponse au manque.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p097","rw":"Uko ugira abandi ni ko bakugira","en":"As you treat others, so they treat you.","fr":"Comme tu traites les autres, ils te traitent aussi.","meaning":"Respect tends to return to the one who gives it.","meaningRw":"Kubaha abandi akenshi bigarukira ukubaha.","meaningFr":"Le respect revient souvent a celui qui le donne.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p098","rw":"Nta byera ngo de","en":"Nothing is ever perfectly white.","fr":"Rien n'est parfaitement blanc.","meaning":"Every situation has limits and imperfections.","meaningRw":"Buri kintu kigira aho kigarukira n'inenge zacyo.","meaningFr":"Chaque situation a ses limites et ses imperfections.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p099","rw":"Uwanze kumva ntiyanze kubona","en":"Who refuses to listen has not refused to see.","fr":"Qui refuse d'ecouter n'a pas refuse de voir.","meaning":"Experience will teach those who reject advice.","meaningRw":"Uwanze inama azigishwa n'ibyo azabona.","meaningFr":"L'experience instruit celui qui refuse le conseil.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"},
    {"id":"p100","rw":"Ufashe hasi agera kure","en":"Who starts low reaches far.","fr":"Qui commence bas va loin.","meaning":"Humility and steady beginnings can lead to success.","meaningRw":"Kwicisha bugufi no gutangira buhoro bishobora kugeza umuntu kure.","meaningFr":"L'humilite et les debuts patients menent loin.","source":"Rwandan oral tradition"}
  ]
}
```

  "ibisakuzo": [

// data/stories/gihanga.js
//
// Full story content for "Gihanga Ngomijana" — the founding king of Rwanda.
// Same shape as data/stories/ruganzu.js, so it can be dropped into Discover.jsx,
// the story library, or StoryReadModal.jsx without any changes to those components.
//
// Framed throughout as oral tradition ("the elders say", "it is told") rather than
// settled fact — Gihanga's historicity is itself debated by scholars, and the story
// has been carried by generations of court poets and elders rather than a single
// written record. Keep that framing if you expand this.

import GihangaImg from '../../assets/collections/royal-court.jpg';
// Using the existing royal-court image as a placeholder — it already fits the
// "founding/royal history" theme. Swap this for a dedicated Gihanga or Buhanga
// Sacred Forest image whenever you have one; nothing else needs to change.

export const gihangaStory = {
  id: 'gihanga-ngomijana',
  title: 'Gihanga Ngomijana',
  category: 'Founding history',
  explorerCategory: 'royal', // matches EXPLORER_CATEGORY['royal-historian'] in Home.jsx
  location: 'Buhanga Sacred Forest',
  image: GihangaImg,
  xpReward: 60,
  desc: 'The founder-king said to have descended from the sky, and the fire he lit that was meant to never go out.',
  content: [
    `Before there were kings counted one after another, before there was a name for the land itself, the elders say there was only Gihanga — the one whose name comes from guhanga, "to create." Every story about how Rwanda came to be a kingdom begins, in one way or another, with him. He is remembered less as a man who was born and grew old like other men, and more as the moment a scattered people first became a nation with a name.`,

    `As it is told, his line reached back further than any ordinary ancestry — through his father's side to a distant forefather named Kigwa, "the one who descended," said to have come down from the heavens themselves to plant the royal line on earth. Whether the storyteller means this as memory or as metaphor for something too important to describe plainly has never mattered as much as what came after: a family marked, from its very beginning, as meant to lead.`,

    `Gihanga's own childhood was not an easy one. He was born, the elders say, in a time of disaster, and lost his father while still young. His mother carried him to her own grandfather's home, and it was there — away from where he might otherwise have been raised — that he grew into a boy so clever and so promising that he became his grandfather's favorite. A prophecy began to follow him quietly: that the throne of his forefathers would one day be his.`,

    `A promise like that rarely goes unchallenged. His maternal uncle, watching the boy rise in favor and hearing the same prophecy repeated, was consumed by envy rather than pride. Rather than wait to see whether the prophecy was true, he began to scheme against the nephew who stood to inherit what he himself could not. Gihanga, still young, fled his uncle's reach together with a handful of loyal cousins — the first of several journeys that would carry him across unfamiliar territory before he ever ruled anything at all.`,

    `It was in his wandering, not in a palace, that Gihanga became the figure Rwandans still speak of today. Wherever he went, the stories say, he brought knowledge that a scattered people badly needed — the forging of iron, the shaping of wood, the working of clay into pottery, the keeping of fire, the raising of cattle. He was not only a claimant to a throne; he was, by every account, a craftsman first — a blacksmith's son who had learned his father's trade and carried it with him like a second inheritance.`,

    `He eventually made his way to Buhanga, a forest that would come to be remembered as sacred ground, and it was there that the scattered pieces of his journey became a kingdom. It was in Buhanga that he is said to have performed the rituals that marked his rule as legitimate, and where his first royal symbols were set — a hammer, for the craft that had carried him this far, and a musical instrument whose call was said to be able to seal the fate of the condemned. Later, tradition holds, one of his companions revealed to him the secret of a sacred royal drum — the beginning of what would become the Kalinga, the drum that would define Rwandan kingship for centuries afterward.`,

    `Perhaps the most enduring symbol of all was the fire Gihanga lit at his court — a flame that, once kindled, was never meant to go out. For generations after him, it did not: kept burning through the reigns of kings who came long after his name had passed from memory into legend, a living sign that the kingdom he founded still stood. It would take colonial officials, centuries later, to finally order it extinguished — an act many Rwandans still describe not merely as political, but as an attempt to sever something the fire had always represented: an unbroken line between a people and their beginning.`,

    `Gihanga's story does not end tidily with a single victory or a single throne. It survives instead in fragments carried by different families, different clans, different court poets — some claiming descent from a son who inherited his kingdom, others from a daughter said to have brought the first cattle to Rwanda after a family dispute of her own. That every version disagrees on some detail and agrees on the shape of the whole is, in its own way, exactly how a founding story should survive: not as one fixed account, but as something every generation retells a little differently, because it still belongs to all of them.`,
  ].join('\n\n'),
  quiz: [
    {
      question: "What does the name 'Gihanga' mean?",
      options: ["The one who descended", "To create", "The blacksmith", "The warrior"],
      correctIndex: 1,
      explanation: "Gihanga comes from the word 'guhanga', which means 'to create'."
    },
    {
      question: "Which of the following crafts is Gihanga said to have brought to his people?",
      options: ["Weaving and farming", "Forging iron and shaping wood", "Building stone walls", "Writing"],
      correctIndex: 1,
      explanation: "He brought the knowledge of forging iron, shaping wood, working clay, keeping fire, and raising cattle."
    },
    {
      question: "What was the significance of the fire Gihanga lit at his court?",
      options: ["It was used to forge weapons", "It was meant to never go out", "It warned enemies", "It was only lit during festivals"],
      correctIndex: 1,
      explanation: "The fire was meant to never go out, representing an unbroken line between the people and their beginning."
    }
  ]
};

export default gihangaStory;

### `src/data/stories/inanga.js`

```javascript
// data/stories/inanga.js
//
// Full story content about the Inanga — Rwanda's most revered traditional
// instrument — anchored around the real historical king Yuhi III Mazimpaka,
// remembered as a poet and inanga player. Same shape as the other story files.
//
// Unlike Ryangombe or Gihanga, this one leans on documented cultural history
// rather than pure legend — Mazimpaka's reputation as a poet-king is
// recorded in Rwandan oral and court-poetry tradition (ibitekerezo). Keep
// that same grounded, factual tone if this story is expanded.

import InangaImg from '../../assets/home/inanga.jpg';

export const inangaStory = {
  id: 'inanga-mazimpaka',
  title: 'The Inanga and the Poet-King',
  category: 'Traditional music',
  location: 'Nyanza Royal Court',
  image: InangaImg,
  xpReward: 45,
  explorerCategory: 'music', // matches EXPLORER_CATEGORY['music-explorer'] in Home.jsx
  desc: 'How a single string, threaded back and forth across a wooden trough, became the sound of Rwanda\'s royal court.',
  content: [
    `Long before speakers and stages, the sound that carried Rwanda's history was startlingly simple: one long string, threaded back and forth across notches cut into a hollowed wooden trough, plucked by a single pair of hands. That instrument is the inanga, and for centuries it has been considered one of the most revered instruments in Rwandan life — not because of volume or complexity, but because of what it was trusted to carry: memory itself.`,

    `The inanga's design hides its cleverness in plain sight. What looks like six to eight separate strings is often just one continuous length, woven across a series of carved notches at either end of the trough, then tuned string by string with small wooden pegs. Seated with the instrument resting against the lap, a player plucks out a repeating, pentatonic melody — and it's over that gentle, looping foundation that the real performance begins: a voice, half-sung and half-whispered, carrying stories of history, personal experience, or the ordinary events of daily life.`,

    `In Rwanda's royal courts, the inanga held a place few instruments anywhere are given — it was played for kings, trusted to praise them, and trusted just as often to record them. Among the names still remembered from that tradition is Yuhi III Mazimpaka, a king of the early eighteenth century remembered less for conquest than for a rarer kind of reputation: a brilliant poet and skilled musician in his own right, said to have used his gift to tell the story of his own kingdom's rise.`,

    `That a king would be remembered as a performer, rather than only as a ruler, says something about how central this tradition was to Rwandan court life. The inanga wasn't background music — it was one of the primary ways history moved from one generation to the next, through ibitekerezo, epic poems recounting the deeds of kings and dynasties, composed and performed with the same instrument used for quieter, personal songs about love, loss, or the passing of ordinary days.`,

    `The whispery, murmuring singing style that traditionally accompanies the inanga — sometimes called kwivuga — was deliberately understated, almost private, even when performed for a king. Listeners didn't always catch every word; the lyrics often carried layered or hidden meanings meant to be interpreted rather than simply heard. In many ways, the instrument's quiet character was the point: history told gently is still history remembered.`,

    `The inanga's story didn't end with the royal courts. It survived colonization, cultural upheaval, and — after 1994 — the task of helping a country rebuild a shared cultural identity in the wake of unimaginable loss. Musicians like Thomas Kirusu and his daughter Sophie Nzayisenga, among Rwanda's most celebrated inanga players in recent generations, carried the instrument forward into a new era, proving it could hold both grief and unity in the same strings that once praised kings.`,

    `Today the inanga still rests in players' laps the same way it did centuries ago, still tuned by hand, still accompanied by that same soft, half-sung voice. It remains, as it always has, less an instrument for performance and more a vessel — one string, threaded back and forth, carrying forward whatever a person trusts it to remember.`,
  ].join('\n\n'),
};

export default inangaStory;
```

### `src/data/stories/index.js`

```javascript
// data/stories/index.js
//
// Central library of all written stories. Used by Home.jsx as the LOCAL
// fallback for the personalized "highlight" card while the real backend
// endpoint (/api/heritage?category=...) doesn't exist yet. Once that backend
// is live, it takes priority automatically — this file only fills the gap
// until then, and keeps working afterward as a safety net if that request
// ever fails or returns nothing.

import { gihangaStory } from './gihanga';
import { nyirarucyabaStory } from './nyirarucyaba';
import { ruganzuStory } from './ruganzu';
import { kigeliStory } from './kigeli';
import { ryangombeStory } from './ryangombe';
import { inangaStory } from './inanga';

export const ALL_STORIES = [
  gihangaStory,
  nyirarucyabaStory,
  ruganzuStory,
  kigeliStory,
  ryangombeStory,
  inangaStory,
];

/**
 * Returns the best local story to show as the dashboard's "Today's Highlight"
 * for a given explorer category ('warrior' | 'nature' | 'royal' | 'folklore' | 'music').
 *
 * Every explorer type now has at least one matching story:
 *   warrior          → Ruganzu II Ndoli, Kigeli IV Rwabugiri
 *   royal-historian  → Gihanga Ngomijana
 *   folktale-hunter  → Nyirarucyaba
 *   nature-lover     → Ryangombe
 *   music-explorer   → The Inanga and the Poet-King
 */
export function getHighlightForCategory(category) {
  const match = ALL_STORIES.find((s) => s.explorerCategory === category);
  return match || ALL_STORIES[0];
}

export default ALL_STORIES;
```

### `src/data/stories/kigeli.js`

```javascript
// data/stories/kigeli.js
//
// Full story content for "Kigeli IV Rwabugiri" — the last great warrior king
// of the Nyiginya dynasty. Same shape as ruganzu.js / gihanga.js.
//
// Historical note for whoever edits this later: unlike Gihanga or Ruganzu,
// Rwabugiri's reign (1853–1895) is well documented in written record, not just
// oral tradition — so this one leans slightly more factual/historical in tone
// rather than "as the elders say". His reign also included harsher chapters
// (forced labor under the land-redistribution system he introduced) — this
// telling doesn't erase that, but keeps the tone educational rather than
// dwelling on it, since the story's focus is his life and reputation, not
// a political argument. Handle any further edits to this period carefully.

import KigeliImg from '../../assets/home/kigeli.jpg';

export const kigeliStory = {
  id: 'kigeli-iv-rwabugiri',
  title: 'Kigeli IV Rwabugiri',
  category: 'Royal history',
  explorerCategory: 'warrior', // matches EXPLORER_CATEGORY['warrior'] in Home.jsx — his reign was defined by conquest
  location: 'Lake Kivu',
  image: KigeliImg,
  xpReward: 55,
  desc: 'The last great warrior king of Rwanda, whose conquests carried the kingdom to the largest borders it would ever hold.',
  content: [
    `By the time Kigeli IV Rwabugiri took the throne in 1853, the kingdom his ancestors had built over centuries — reaching all the way back to Gihanga, the founder himself — had grown large, but not yet as large as it would become under him. Born Sezisoni Rwabugiri, son of Mutara II Rwogera, he would spend the whole of his reign proving that the dynasty's oldest ideal — kwanda, to expand — still had one more chapter left to write.`,

    `He earned his reputation the way Rwandan kings before him always had: on campaign. Expedition followed expedition, year after year, until his name carried titles meant to be sung rather than simply spoken — Inkotanyi cyane among them, "the truly relentless." Elders who remembered his era compared his bravery to Ruganzu II Ndoli's, the king who had crossed the Nyabarongo two centuries before him. It was rare praise, reserved for a king who was said to treat the battlefield the way other men treated their own home.`,

    `His campaigns reached further than any king before him — west toward Lake Kivu, where he fought for control of Ijwi Island and its ruler Kabego; south into Bugesera; east toward kingdoms that had never answered to Rwanda before. Each victory folded new land, new cattle, and new subjects into a kingdom that, by the time his reign ended, stretched to the widest borders it would ever hold. He built a lakeside residence at Nyamasheke, from where the campaigns against Kivu's islands were planned — a war room with a view of the water he meant to conquer.`,

    `Rwabugiri did not only fight; he rebuilt what he ruled. He reorganized the army into standing units — the elite Intore among them — replacing loose levies with something closer to a professional fighting force. He redrew the kingdom's map into provinces, districts, and hills, each answering to chiefs he appointed himself, and split the old duties of land and cattle management so that no single chief could grow powerful enough to rival the throne. It was, in its way, the most centralized Rwanda had ever been.`,

    `He was also the first Rwandan king to stand face to face with Europeans arriving on his borders — explorers, then traders, then the beginnings of colonial ambition. He met them carefully: taking German firearms to arm his own soldiers, while barring most other foreigners, including Arab traders, from entering his kingdom at all. He meant to use what the outside world offered without letting it in any further than that — a balancing act few kings anywhere in the region managed as long as he did.`,

    `It would be incomplete to tell this story only as one of glory. The same reforms that centralized his rule also reshaped how ordinary Rwandans lived on the land — introducing a system where appointed Tutsi chiefs demanded labor from Hutu families in exchange for the right to farm it, a patronage system that hardened social lines in ways that would echo long after Rwabugiri himself was gone. A full account of his reign holds both things at once: the warrior-king who carried Rwanda to its widest borders, and the ruler whose reforms left divisions his successors — and the country itself — would spend generations reckoning with.`,

    `Rwabugiri died in 1895, on campaign as he had lived, and is remembered by many as the last true king of the old Nyiginya line — his death followed swiftly by a palace coup that installed a very different kind of rule. What survived him wasn't only territory. It was a reputation carried in songs composed in his own lifetime, praising his relentlessness, and a kingdom whose shape — for better and for worse — still marks the outline of Rwanda today.`,
  ].join('\n\n'),
  quiz: [
    {
      question: "Which of the following kings was Kigeli IV Rwabugiri's father?",
      options: ["Gihanga Ngomijana", "Ruganzu II Ndoli", "Mutara II Rwogera", "Musinga"],
      correctIndex: 2,
      explanation: "He was born Sezisoni Rwabugiri, son of Mutara II Rwogera."
    },
    {
      question: "What does 'Inkotanyi cyane' mean?",
      options: ["The truly relentless", "The great king", "The conqueror", "The first warrior"],
      correctIndex: 0,
      explanation: "He earned the title 'Inkotanyi cyane' meaning 'the truly relentless' due to his constant campaigns."
    },
    {
      question: "How did Kigeli IV Rwabugiri reform the military?",
      options: ["He disbanded the military", "He reorganized the army into standing units like the Intore", "He relied solely on mercenaries", "He created a navy on Lake Kivu"],
      correctIndex: 1,
      explanation: "He reorganized the army into standing units—the elite Intore among them—replacing loose levies with a professional fighting force."
    }
  ]
};

export default kigeliStory;
```

### `src/data/stories/nyirarucyaba.js`

```javascript
// data/stories/nyirarucyaba.js
//
// Full story content for "Nyirarucyaba" — Gihanga's daughter, credited in
// Rwandan folklore with bringing the first cattle to the kingdom. A natural
// companion piece to gihanga.js: same generation, same founding era, but a
// smaller, gentler story with a woman at its center rather than a king.
// Same shape as the other story files.

import NyirarucyabaImg from '../../assets/international/umuganura.jpg';
// Using the existing Umuganura (harvest festival) image as a placeholder —
// it fits the agricultural/pastoral theme. Swap for a dedicated image
// (e.g. of Mount Kabuye, or cattle) whenever you have one.

export const nyirarucyabaStory = {
  id: 'nyirarucyaba',
  title: 'Nyirarucyaba',
  category: 'Founding history',
  explorerCategory: 'folklore', // matches EXPLORER_CATEGORY['folktale-hunter'] in Home.jsx
  location: 'Mount Kabuye',
  image: NyirarucyabaImg,
  xpReward: 45,
  desc: 'Gihanga\'s daughter, and the woman said to have brought the first cattle to the Kingdom of Rwanda.',
  content: [
    `Not every founding story in Rwanda belongs to a king. Some of the oldest and gentlest ones belong to the women standing just beside the throne — and few are told as fondly as the story of Nyirarucyaba, daughter of Gihanga, the founder-king himself. Where her father's story is one of thrones and prophecies, hers is a smaller story, about a single household and a single unfamiliar animal — and yet it is the story Rwandans still credit for one of the most treasured things in their culture: the cow.`,

    `As it is told, Nyirarucyaba did not grow up in easy peace. A dispute arose between her mother, Nyamususa, and her stepmother, Nyirampirangwe — the kind of household rivalry that, in a royal family, could turn dangerous quickly. Nyirarucyaba defended her mother fiercely, so fiercely that she feared what punishment might follow. Rather than wait to find out, she fled her childhood home, the way so many figures in these old stories do, carrying little more than her own resolve.`,

    `She found her way eventually to a quieter life, marrying a farmer named Kazigaba and settling far from the disputes of court. It is here, in this small and unremarkable household, that the story turns from family drama into legend. One day, the elders say, an animal neither of them recognized arrived at their home — unlike anything they had kept or seen before. The next day, it gave birth.`,

    `Nyirarucyaba noticed something else strange: a liquid dripping from the animal, one she had never encountered. Curious rather than afraid, she investigated it herself, and carried what she found back to her father's court — not as a report, but as a gift. She brought Gihanga the milk.`,

    `The king, the story goes, was relieved simply by the taste of it — and understood immediately that this was no ordinary discovery. He ordered his servants to retrieve these animals for the kingdom itself, and it is from that single household's unfamiliar visitor that Rwandan tradition traces the beginning of cattle-keeping across the land. Mount Kabuye, in what is now Gakenke District, is remembered as the place that sheltered Nyirarucyaba and her cattle in the years that followed.`,

    `It's worth pausing on why this particular story has lasted as long as it has. Cattle in Rwanda were never simply livestock — they became wealth, status, poetry, and ceremony, celebrated in songs and central to marriage customs and royal ritual alike for centuries afterward. That such a foundational part of Rwandan life is credited not to a conquest or a divine descent, but to one woman's curiosity and generosity toward her father, says something the grander stories of kings and battles rarely do: that some of the most enduring gifts a culture carries began as something quietly noticed, and freely given.`,
  ].join('\n\n'),
  quiz: [

Between Ruganzu and the court that had once been his stood the Nyabarongo — a river that Rwandans have long treated as more than water, a boundary between what a person was and what they were about to become. Ruganzu answered each test the same way he had answered the river: not with declarations, but with presence. He stayed. He listened. He did not flinch twice.`,

      `In time, the doubts gave way to something else — the recognition that the kingdom he had returned to needed exactly the kind of steadiness he had shown at its edge. Under his rule, as the oral histories describe it, Rwanda's reach and its confidence both grew. Ruganzu is remembered less for a single victory than for a temperament: a king who had already survived being erased once, and who ruled afterward like a man who understood, more than most, what it cost a people to lose their place and what it took to reclaim it.`,

It is told as a lesson about return: that the home you were taken from can still be reached, that doubt is not the same as defeat, and that sometimes the most important thing a person can do is simply refuse to turn back at the water's edge.`,

      `The story of Ruganzu II Ndoli belongs to no single version — griots, grandparents, and now digital archives like this one all carry it a little differently, each shaped by the voice that passed it on. Abakuru b'inkuru bavuga ko umugezi wari muremure kandi utemera ku munsi yageze ku nkengero zabyo, nk'aho n'ubutaka bwashyaga kwemeza ko uyu muhungu w'ubwami wari ubutaye amatwi akwiye kugaruka iwe. Ariko buri verisiyo yemera icyo cyakurikiye: ntiyaje mu bwumvikane. Ubutumwa bw'umuhungu w'ubwami wambutse Nyabarongo atatinya bwanyura mu misozi byaruta uko yajyaga, bugera mu ngoro mbere y'uko ashyira ikirenge muri yo. Ruganzu yasubije buri gerageza mu buryo bwe bwasubije umugezi: atavuga amagambo, ahubwo ariho. Yari ariho. Yumvaga. Ntiyatinya kabiri.`,

      `Muri make, amagambo yahindutse ikindi kintu — kumenya ko ubwami yari agarutseho bari uko bwashatse uko yari yerekanye ku mpande zabyo.       `Longtemps avant que les collines du Rwanda ne portent des routes et des fils électriques, elles portaient des noms — et peu de noms sont racontés autour du feu aussi souvent que Ruganzu II Ndoli. Il grandit parmi des étrangers, dans une maison qui n'était pas la sienne, élevé moins dans le confort que dans une seule promise répétée à voix basse, année après année : que les collines dont on l'avait arraché attendaient toujours leur héritier légitime.`,

      `Les histoires disent que l'exil fait deux choses à un prince — soit il l'efface, soit il le forge. Pour Ruganzu, ce fut la seconde. Au moment où la nouvelle lui parvint que le trône de ses ancêtres était chancelant, il n'était plus l'enfant effrayé qui l'avait quitté. C'était un jeune homme qui avait passé sa vie à attendre précisément ce moment, et qui n'avait plus rien à perdre en le saisissant.`,

      `Son retour, comme on le raconte, n'allait pas être simple. Entre Ruganzu et la cour qui avait autrefois été la sienne se dressait la Nyabarongo — une rivière que les Rwandais ont longtemps traitée comme plus que de l'eau, une frontière entre ce qu'une personne était et ce qu'elle était sur le point de devenir. Les anciens qui ont conservé cette histoire disent que la rivière était haute et peu accueillante le jour où il atteignit ses rives, comme si la terre elle-même avait besoin d'être convaincue que ce fils exilé méritait de rentrer chez lui. Certains qui voyageaient avec lui hésitèrent au bord de l'eau. Ruganzu, non.`,

      `Il traversa. Ce qui exactement le porta de l'autre côté — courage, conviction, ou le simple refus de faire demi-tour après tant d'années d'attente — dépend de qui raconte l'histoire dans le village. Mais toutes les versions s'accordent sur ce qui vint après : il n'arriva pas silencieusement. La nouvelle d'un prince qui avait traversé la Nyabarongo sans flancher se propagea dans les collines plus vite que lui, atteignant la cour avant qu'il n'y ait jamais mis le pied. Au moment où il arriva, il n'était plus seulement un nom que les gens se souvenaient vaguement. Il était déjà en train de devenir une histoire.`,

      `Tout le monde à la cour ne l'accueillit pas. Les anciens décrivent de longues saisons d'épreuves — des doutes chuchotés sur la capacité du garçon qui était parti si longtemps à vraiment diriger, des défis discrets destinés à voir si sa résolution au bord de la rivière avait été un acte unique de bravoure ou quelque chose qu'il pouvait soutenir. Ruganzu répondit à chaque épreuve de la même manière qu'il avait répondu à la rivière : non pas par des déclarations, mais par sa présence. Il resta. Il écouta. Il ne flancha pas deux fois.`,

      `Avec le temps, les doutes firent place à autre chose — la reconnaissance que le royaume qu'il avait rejoint avait précisément besoin de la stabilité qu'il avait montrée à sa frontière. Ruganzu est moins rappelé pour une victoire unique que pour un tempérament : un roi qui avait déjà survécu à l'effacement une fois, et qui régna par la suite comme un homme qui comprenait, plus que la plupart, ce que coûte à un peuple de perdre sa place et ce qu'il faut pour la reconquérir.`,

      `Ce qui a porté son nom à travers tant de générations de conteurs n'est pas seulement la traversée elle-même, mais ce qu'elle est venue représenter. Elle est racontée comme une leçon sur le retour : que la maison dont on vous a arraché peut toujours être atteinte, que le doute n'est pas la même chose que la défaite, et que parfois la chose la plus importante qu'une personne puisse faire est simplement refuser de faire demi-tour au bord de l'eau.`,

      `L'histoire de Ruganzu II Ndoli n'appartient à aucune version unique — les griots, les grands-parents, et maintenant les archives numériques comme celle-ci la portent tous un peu différemment, chacun façonné par la voix qui l'a transmise. C'est, à sa manière, la chose la plus vraie à son sujet : une histoire aussi ancienne ne survit pas en restant exactement la même, mais en étant racontée encore et encore, par quiconque a besoin de l'entendre ensuite.`,

### `src/data/stories/ryangombe.js`

```javascript
// data/stories/ryangombe.js
//
// Full story content for "Ryangombe" — the hunter-hero of Rwandan oral
// tradition, whose legend is closely tied to forests, wilderness, and the
// Virunga volcanoes. Same shape as the other story files.
//
// Careful note for whoever edits this: Ryangombe is the central figure of
// Kubandwa, a real spiritual tradition still honored by some communities
// today — this isn't a purely historical legend the way Gihanga or Ruganzu
// are. This telling deliberately stays respectful and focuses on Ryangombe's
// role as a nature/hunter figure (which is what makes him fit the
// "nature-lover" explorer type), and leaves out the more mature or
// contested elements found in some fuller academic tellings of his myth
// (details around his son Binego, and later colonial-era political
// readings of the cult). If you expand this story, keep that same care —
// treat it as living heritage, not just folklore trivia.

import RyangombeImg from '../../assets/explore/buhanga.jpg';
// Using the existing Buhanga forest image as a placeholder — fits the
// wilderness theme. Swap for a dedicated forest/Virunga volcano image
// (Karisimbi or Muhabura) whenever you have one.

export const ryangombeStory = {
  id: 'ryangombe',
  title: 'Ryangombe',
  category: 'Nature & legend',
  location: 'Virunga Volcanoes',
  image: RyangombeImg,
  xpReward: 50,
  explorerCategory: 'nature', // matches EXPLORER_CATEGORY['nature-lover'] in Home.jsx
  desc: 'The legendary hunter said to have become one with the forest — and with the volcano where his story still lives.',
  content: [
    `Of all the figures carried through Rwanda's oral tradition, none belongs to the wild places quite like Ryangombe. Where kings are remembered for courts and conquests, Ryangombe is remembered for forests, hunts, and mountains — a hero whose whole story unfolds not behind palace walls, but out among the hills, the game trails, and the volcanoes that still rise along Rwanda's northern border.`,

    `The elders say he came originally from Kitara, in what is now western Uganda, arriving in Rwanda generations ago as a young man already known for his skill in the hunt. He was not born into the throne the way Rwanda's kings were — his reputation was built entirely out in the wilderness, tracking game through forest and grassland until his name for courage and skill traveled faster than he did.`,

    `It was on one such hunt, the story goes, that everything changed. Deep in a forest, Ryangombe is said to have come upon a sacred grove unlike any other — a place where the boundary between the ordinary world and something older and larger grew thin. There, spirits are said to have recognized in him a kind of greatness the forest itself had been waiting for, and offered him a place among them.`,

    `What makes Ryangombe's story endure isn't a single act of bravery, but the way he is remembered afterward — as jovial rather than distant, fond of music, dance, and feasting as much as the hunt, a spirit closer to the people who honored him than the fiercer, more fearsome figures found in other traditions. Communities who kept his memory alive did so not out of fear, but out of a sense that he understood the wild world better than almost anyone, and could be trusted to look after those who respected it.`,

    `His story ends, as many old hunting tales do, out in the field — struck down during a hunt, his companions said to have grieved him so deeply that his memory was carried forward not as an ending, but as a beginning. From that day, the elders say, Ryangombe made his home in Karisimbi, one of the great Virunga volcanoes that still stand along Rwanda's northern edge — visible, on a clear day, from almost anywhere in the country.`,

    `That detail is worth sitting with for a moment: of all the places a legendary figure could be said to dwell, Ryangombe's story chose a volcano — visible, permanent, part of the landscape itself. For generations, communities who honored his memory treated Karisimbi the way some cultures treat a temple spire: a constant, shared point on the horizon, a reminder that some stories don't need walls to be remembered. Even now, some communities continue to honor traditions connected to his memory, a living thread between old forests and the present day.`,

    `Whatever else his story carries, the throughline is this: Ryangombe belonged to the wild places first, and only became a legend because he refused to be separated from them. For anyone drawn to Rwanda's forests, hills, and volcanoes today, his story is a reminder that this landscape has always been more than scenery — it has been, for as long as these stories have been told, a place people believed was watching back.`,
  ].join('\n\n'),
};

export default ryangombeStory;
```
